slices.label: Men outside the South
slices.source: 1840 census interpolated toward 1850 to November 1844, free white men 20+ outside the eleven later-Confederate states; property tests had largely gone (Rhode Island's freehold test was relaxed for native-born men in 1843) and a few New England states let free Black men vote; calibrated to certified returns.

slices.label: Women outside the South
slices.source: No women could vote for president in 1844; women 20+ (1840 census interpolated to 1844) are shown for population only.

slices.label: White Southerners
slices.source: 1840 census interpolated to 1844, free white adults in the eleven later-Confederate states; white men voted except in South Carolina, whose legislature chose its electors; calibrated to certified returns.

slices.label: Black Southerners, most of them enslaved
slices.source: 1840 census interpolated to 1844, Black adults in the eleven later-Confederate states, overwhelmingly enslaved; enslaved people could not vote and no Southern state let free Black men vote.

slices.label: Immigrants not yet citizens
slices.source: Estimate only: nativity was first recorded in 1850, so the foreign-born count is back-projected from the 1850 census and arrival records; naturalized men could vote, aliens could not.

runs.summary: Rerun with nothing changed, 1844 comes out as it did: Polk wins, 170–105. The closest state was Tennessee, which went to Clay by 0.1 points. Every one of my 100 reruns reproduces it exactly.
howIGotThis: The numbers: the 1840 and 1850 census counts interpolated to 1844 and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1844 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.

everyone.summary: 6.6 million more adults vote. Connecticut, Delaware, Georgia, Kentucky and 8 more flip, but Polk still wins, 236–39. The closest call is Virginia, which holds for Polk by 0.0 points. Clay wins in 1 of 100 draws.

south-white.name: Anna Reed
south-white.quote: I cannot vote—the law does not allow it. My husband and I may discuss the election, but the choice is his to make, not mine.
south-white.controlQuote: I cannot vote—the law does not allow it. My husband and I may discuss the election, but the choice is his to make, not mine.

women.name: Ruth Robinson
women.quote: I can't vote myself, but my husband will decide between them come election day.
women.controlQuote: I can't vote myself, but my husband will decide between them come election day.

men.name: Ernest Reed
men.quote: The tariff keeps the mills running and wages up. That's what matters to a working man like me. Though I confess this Texas business worries me some.
